title: Why do certain sounds give us chills?
subtitle: Music & brain
subject: sciences
description: Goosebumps, tingles, racing heart: music can hijack our circuits of pleasure and survival. Here's why.

hero.hook: One note, and the skin bristles. The music just hacked your survival brain.

blocks.text: Around **55 to 70%** of people feel chills to music: goosebumps, tingling, rush of emotion. We talk about **aesthetic thrill**, or *chill* in English.
It's not just a picture. Sound waves trigger a real chemical storm in the brain, using circuits designed for survival... and diverted towards beauty.

sections.title: The same circuit as the reward

blocks.text: When a piece “hits”, the brain activates its **reward system**, the network of zones linked to pleasure, the same as for food, sex… or certain drugs. **brain imaging**, techniques that visualize brain activity, shows two stages: first **anticipation**, with **dopamine**, the pleasure neurotransmitter, while we wait for the strong moment; then the thrill itself, when the pleasure bursts.

The chemical proof: **naltrexone**, a drug that blocks **opioid receptors**, natural pleasure molecules, can almost erase musical pleasure. The brain therefore produces its own internal “drugs” to reward an aesthetic experience.
Around **5 %** of people experience no pleasure from music despite normal hearing. We're talking about **musical anhedonia**, the inability to feel pleasure from music.

sections.title: The surprise that makes you shiver

blocks.text: The thrill is often born from a . The brain continually predicts the next note. A chorus that enters too early, a **modulation**, an unexpected change in tone, a tension that takes time to resolve: the emotional alert goes off. [[violation of musical expectation]]

The **amygdala**, a deep area of ​​the brain linked to danger, reacts for a fraction of a second. Goosebumps are an old reflex: raising your hair to appear taller or keep warm. Then the cortex understands that it's art, not a threat. Relief becomes intense pleasure.
Goosebumps are called **piloerection**, the raising of the hairs. In modern humans, music triggers it especially on sad or melancholy passages.

sections.title: Why are some people more sensitive to it?

blocks.text: The researcher  showed that people prone to shivering often have more connections, the **white matter**, fibers that connect areas of the brain, between the auditory cortex, the prefrontal cortex and the **insula**, the area for integrating emotions. Their brain connects sound and feeling more directly. [[Matthew Sachs]]

This trait also goes with the : curiosity, taste for complexity and ambiguity. The more we welcome the unexpected, the more opportunities the brain has to trigger its reward. [[Openness to experience (personality)]]

Darwinianly, musical thrill is a paradox: it does not directly nourish or protect. But synchronizing the emotions of a group could promote **social cohesion**. The frequencies that strike the most also recall tears or cries of distress: urgency first, beauty then.
Basically, music hacks ancient systems to offer one of the most corporeal experiences in art: a vibration of the air that becomes a sensation on the skin.
Musical thrills arise from a release of dopamine triggered by a harmonic surprise, especially in brains that are very connected between hearing and emotion.
